title: Deconstructing Partitiviridae proteins reveals the evolutionary determinants behind their origin and ecological breadth.
abstract: Viruses represent a primary source of biological diversity, yet the specific mechanisms by which viral proteins shape host range remain unclear. Members of the family Partitiviridae offer a minimalist model to address this question: despite their collectively broad host range, they typically encode only an RNA-dependent RNA polymerase (RdRP) and a capsid protein (CP). Here, we integrate sequence phylogenetics with structural analyses of solved and AlphaFold-predicted structures for both proteins to reconstruct their evolutionary trajectories. We show that CPs feature a conserved Reo-like shell core alongside a genus-specific, highly variable protrusion (P) domain. Similarly, the RdRP retains a conserved catalytic core, with terminal variations giving rise to additional elements within the finger domain. Evolutionary analysis indicates that these two proteins originated independently: an ancestral Betapartitivirus-like RdRP triggered the origin of partitiviruses, while a repurposed totivirus-like CP provided the original capsid-traces of which remain evident in Epsilonpartitivirus. Furthermore, structural and phylogenetic similarities reveal subclusters within established genera and suggest three independent insertion events shaping the P domain. Ultimately, this detailed dual-protein framework demonstrates how structural minimalism and modular adaptability facilitate viral survival and cross-kingdom spread, providing a structural explanation for the exceptional ecological breadth of partitiviruses.

title: The complete mitochondrial genome of oil palm pest, Metisa plana (Lepidoptera: Psychidae) and its comparison with other Psychidae species.
abstract: The Malaysian oil palm industry faces significant productivity losses from insect pests, making genetic characterization essential for effective pest control. Mitochondrial genomes (mitogenomes) offer critical insights into pest evolution, population dynamics, and insecticide resistance. Here, we present the complete 16,795 bp mitogenome of Metisa plana Walker, a major oil palm foliage pest. It contains the typical insect complement of 13 protein-coding genes (PCGs), 2 ribosomal RNA genes (rRNAs), 22 transfer RNA genes (tRNAs), and a 1,554 bp control region (CR). The mitogenome is highly A + T-biased (81% overall; 99% in the CR). All PCGs initiate with standard ATN codons except COX1 (TCG), while COX2 terminates with a common insect incomplete stop codon. All tRNAs fold into typical cloverleaf secondary structures except trnS1, which lacks the dihydrouridine (DHU) arm. Selective pressure analysis indicates strong purifying selection across all PCGs (Ka/Ks = 0.1001-0.5545). Maximum-likelihood (ML) and Bayesian inference (BI) phylogenetic analyses confirmed the monophyly of Psychidae, placing M. plana adjacent to the "Acanthopsyche-Pachytelia" subclade and in a sister relationship with the "Eumeta-Mahasena" subclade. This mitogenome provides a valuable reference for future phylogenetic studies of Malaysian bagworms and supports improved pest management strategies.

title: From prophylactic mRNA vaccines against viral infections to therapeutic applications: regulatory science considerations for expanding mRNA platforms.
abstract: Conventional non-amplifying messenger RNA (mRNA) and self-amplifying RNA (saRNA) medicines generally share a core linear RNA architecture-including a 5' cap, untranslated regions, one or more open reading frames, and a poly(A) tail-and are commonly formulated with delivery systems such as lipid nanoparticles (LNPs) to enable transient intracellular expression of a target protein. Prophylactic mRNA vaccines are designed primarily to express infectious-disease antigens and generate protective immune memory, whereas mRNA therapeutics exert pharmacological effects intended to treat disease, suppress recurrence, replace proteins, modulate immunity, or deliver gene-editing enzymes. Thus, even products based on similar mRNA-LNP technology may have different regulatory classifications and evidence requirements according to their intended use and mechanism of action. The clinical and regulatory landscape has expanded beyond the first coronavirus disease 2019 vaccines to include respiratory syncytial virus and influenza mRNA vaccines, an influenza-coronavirus disease 2019 combination vaccine, an authorized saRNA vaccine, personalized cancer immunotherapies, protein-replacement therapies, in vivo cell programming, and gene-editing delivery systems. This review examines which prophylactic-vaccine evidence can support therapeutic development and where product-specific quality, nonclinical, clinical, and lifecycle evidence remains necessary. For prophylactic mRNA vaccines, major regulatory considerations include quality, immunogenicity, preventive efficacy, lot release, and safety surveillance after large-scale vaccination. For mRNA therapeutics, the principal issues include delivery to target tissues, function of the expressed product, repeat-dose safety, biodistribution, off-target risk, long-term follow-up, and patient-specific manufacture and traceability. In particular, although personalized mRNA cancer vaccines are commonly described as vaccines, they are closer in regulatory purpose to therapeutics that act on the basis of each patient's tumor characteristics than to vaccines that prevent infectious disease. Antigen-selection algorithms, patient-specific sequence design, small-batch and multi-product manufacture, product-patient matching, clinical evaluation of combination strategies, manufacturing delays and analysis populations, and risk-based long-term postauthorization follow-up therefore require explicit regulatory consideration. Platform-level knowledge from prophylactic mRNA vaccine authorization can support therapeutic development, but regulatory questions may vary with each new product type; developers will need to track evolving regulatory instruments across jurisdictions and engage regulatory authorities early.

title: Early caregiving adversity is associated with elevated pro-inflammatory gene expression during adolescence.
abstract: Early life adversity (ELA) is thought to increase risk for poor health outcomes, in part through induction of a persistent pro-inflammatory phenotype. Though ELA has been consistently associated with elevated circulating markers of inflammation in varied adult populations, meta-analytic work has found mixed links between ELA and circulating protein markers of inflammation in adolescents, leaving the pathways by which the adult inflammatory phenotype emerges unclear. Here we examined whether alterations in pro-inflammatory and Type I interferon (antiviral) gene expression in circulating immune cells (the Conserved Transcriptional Response to Adversity; CTRA) might provide a more sensitive measure of ELA-linked phenotypes in adolescents. We assessed pro-inflammatory (NF-κB) and anti-viral (Interferon Response Factor) transcription factor activity and downstream gene expression in peripheral blood samples from 18 internationally adopted youth who had experienced previous institutional caregiving (a profound form of ELA) and 34 comparison, non-adopted youth. Consistent with the CTRA, relative to comparison youth, youth with a history of ELA showed elevated pro-inflammatory (NF-κB) and decreased antiviral (IRF) transcription factor activity. We found no group differences on a priori downstream gene expression composites. Differentially expressed transcripts were preferentially derived from CD16 + and CD16- monocytes, responsible for coordinating the early inflammatory stages of immune responses. These findings confirm ELA-linked inflammatory gene regulation in circulating blood cells during adolescence. Compared to plasma protein measures, functional genomic (RNA) measures of inflammation may provide more sensitive, early indexes of developmental trajectories of inflammation following adversity, prior to emergence of an adult ELA-linked inflammatory phenotype associated with disease.

title: Construction of a stable T7 expression system inSaccharomyces cerevisiae based on extranuclear replication system.
abstract: The bacteriophage T7 expression system is a powerful tool for recombinant protein production, yet its application in eukaryotes is hindered by nuclear-cytoplasmic compartmentalization and inefficient mRNA export. To circumvent this barrier, we aimed to construct a stable cytoplasmic T7 expression system in Saccharomyces cerevisiae by utilizing the extranuclear replication system based on linear plasmids pGKL1/pGKL2 from Kluyveromyces lactis. We integrated the T7 RNA polymerase gene under control of the constitutive TEF1 promoter into the genome of S. cerevisiae F102-2u, and inserted a T7 expression cassette containing an internal ribosome entry site (IRES) into the cytoplasmic p1 plasmid. The system achieved high-level expression of NanoLuc® luciferase (luminescence intensity ~ 108) comparable to the strong Gal system, and successfully expressed super-folder GFP. Quantitative analysis showed that T7 RNA polymerase exhibited higher transcription efficiency and greater processivity on the p1 plasmid compared to genomic DNA or the 2μ plasmid, with early-stage transcription being up to 100-fold higher than on genomic DNA. The system maintained stable expression over multiple passages under selective pressure. This study establishes a robust cytoplasmic T7 expression system in yeast, resolving the nuclear export issue. It further demonstrates that higher-order DNA structure profoundly influences T7 transcription efficiency. This system provides a novel strategy for efficient protein production and has broad applications in synthetic biology and industrial biotechnology.

title: Conditional Codon-Boundary Dinucleotide Organization in Platycerium Plastomes.
abstract: Synonymous evolution can alter both codon abundance and the placement of synonymous codons within genes. We asked whether plastid coding sequences retain non-random codon-boundary organization after protein sequence and exact codon inventory are held constant. We analysed 44 genes lacking an RNA-editing exception flag in the reference annotation across 18 Platycerium species, using exact-codon conditional randomization as the principal analysis and RSCU comparisons as supporting phylogenetic context. CpG boundaries were depleted across species and most genes, with the direction retained under reconstruction and gene-length sensitivities. TpA showed greater gene-level heterogeneity. Both patterns belonged to a coupled landscape of 16 boundary contexts, in which GpT had the lowest observed/expected ratio. These observations distinguish synonymous placement from codon abundance without identifying the evolutionary processes responsible. Shared ancestry, context-dependent mutation, and local sequence constraints remain compatible explanations. The results establish a boundary-order pattern within the sampled matrix and motivate phylogenetically informed comparisons to distinguish historical retention from continued maintenance or recurrent change.

title: An RNA-targeting ADP-ribosyltransferase toxin uncouples mRNA stability from productive translation.
abstract: Messenger RNA (mRNA) modifications regulate transcript stability and translation efficiency across diverse biological systems, but the consequences of toxin-mediated mRNA modification in bacteria remain poorly understood. RhsP2 was recently identified as an RNA-targeting interbacterial ADP-ribosyltransferase toxin, but whether mRNAs are physiological substrates remained unknown. Here, we show that RhsP2 targets mRNA coding sequences and in doing so prevents their efficient translation. eCLIP-seq reveals preferential association of RhsP2 with UAAG-enriched motifs, and biochemical analyses showed that these sequences are preferred substrates for ribose 2'-OH ADP-ribosylation. Unexpectedly, modified mRNAs were broadly stabilized despite impaired protein synthesis, demonstrating that RhsP2 uncouples transcript stability from productive translation. Monosome- and disome-seq analyses show that RhsP2-modified mRNAs induce ribosome stalling and collision, and in vitro translation reactions demonstrate that ADP-ribosylation of mRNAs is sufficient to block translation elongation. Together, these findings establish mRNA ADP-ribosylation as a mechanism of toxin-mediated translational sabotage in which chemically modified transcripts accumulate while disrupting protein synthesis.

title: Ubiquitination and Deubiquitination: From Molecular Mechanisms to Therapeutic Strategies.
abstract: Ubiquitination and deubiquitination are established as a reversible regulatory system controlling protein stability, localization, molecular interactions, and signaling duration. Ubiquitin is recognized not merely as a proteasomal degradation signal but as a molecular code whose output is determined by substrate identity, chain topology, and cellular context. Distinct ubiquitin signals are generated by E3 ubiquitin ligases (E3 ligases), remodeled by deubiquitinating enzymes (DUBs), and decoded by ubiquitinbinding domains. Beyond protein turnover, epigenetic and epitranscriptomic factors are directly regulated by ubiquitin signaling through control of their stability, activity, and interactions, thereby integrating chromatin and RNA regulation. In this review, the ubiquitin activating enzyme (E1)/ubiquitin conjugating enzyme (E2)/E3 cascade, ubiquitin chain architectures, DUBs, and signal recognition mechanisms are outlined in relation to key biological processes. The contribution of disrupted networks to cancer, neurodegeneration, and autoimmune diseases is discussed. Therapeutic strategies, including proteolysis targeting chimeras (PROTACs), molecular glues, DUB inhibitors, and E3 modulators, are presented with early clinical and preclinical developments highlighted to link mechanistic biology to therapeutic design. Shared principles of degradative and nondegradative ubiquitin signaling are identified across cellular networks, with emphasis on epigenetic and epitranscriptomic regulation. A nuanced framework is offered to interpret disease dysfunction, evaluate targeted therapies, and prioritize unresolved questions regarding substrate specificity and signaling context.

title: Replicating vs. non-replicating RNA therapeutics: Mechanisms, trade-offs, and future directions.
abstract: RNA-based therapies are providing new ways to treat infections, cancer, and inherited diseases. These therapies fall into two broad categories: non-replicating RNAs, like messenger RNA, small interfering RNA (siRNA), and antisense oligonucleotides; and replicating RNAs, such as self-amplifying RNA (saRNA) and defective interfering (DI) RNAs. Non-replicating RNAs act in a single round and depend on precise chemical design and effective delivery. Replicating RNAs make more copies of themselves inside cells directly or conditionally, which can improve their strength, duration, and ability to trigger immune responses. In this review, we compare how these two groups of RNA therapies work, how they are designed and delivered, and where they are best suited. We discuss differences in immune effects, dosing, and manufacturing, and include long-studied DI RNAs, now being developed as a new type of antiviral therapy with broad activity and a favorable emerging preclinical safety profile. We also explore delivery methods such as lipid nanoparticles (LNPs) and polymer-based systems. By comparing replicating and non-replicating strategies, we aim to clarify their roles in RNA medicine and highlight how they might be combined in future treatments.

title: Oocyte lipid damage from maternal ageing marks neurodevelopment in mouse offspring.
abstract: Is advanced maternal age (AMA) associated with lipid dysregulation in oocytes that correlates with the intergenerational persistence of altered lipid homeostasis and neurodevelopmental pathway signatures in downstream offspring? Lipid profile alterations characterized in AMA oocytes are associated with distinct lipidomic and spectral variations in the foetal brain and yolk sac, displaying intergenerational persistence that extends up to the fourth generation (F4), independently of the gestational uterine environment. AMA is a recognized prenatal risk factor for neurodevelopmental conditions in offspring. However, whether early-life oocyte lipid variations correlate with altered lipid profiles and molecular signatures in the developing brains of subsequent generations remain uncharacterized. This controlled animal model study compared oocytes, blastocysts, and foetuses from AMA mice (8-16 months old) to those from young maternal age (YMA, 3-4 months old) controls and featured an embryo transfer (ET) of AMA blastocysts into young surrogates and longitudinal, lineage-specific tracking up to the F4. Complementary approaches, including liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry (LC-MS) proteomics and lipidomics, Matrix-Assisted Laser Desorption/Ionization-Tandem Time-of-Flight mass spectrometry (MALDI-TOF/TOF MS), RNA sequencing, atomic force microscopy, Coherent Anti-Stokes Raman Scattering (CARS) chemical imaging microscopy, Raman and Fourier transform infrared (FTIR) spectroscopies, and histology were conducted on single oocytes, blastocysts, and foetal structures (brain and yolk sac) from AMA and YMA mice. ET was utilized to decouple the oocyte-derived phenotype from the effects of an ageing maternal uterine environment. AMA oocytes and preimplantation blastocysts exhibited significant lipid droplet and lipid membrane alterations, a higher relative absorbance of intracellular lipid bands, and altered expression of lipid-regulatory transcripts, corresponding to early embryonic pathway shifts. Following the ET of AMA blastocysts to young surrogates (ET AMA group), distinct lipidomic variations and structural alterations were observed in the F1 yolk sac and foetal brains. Furthermore, these lipid-associated spectral and molecular signatures displayed intergenerational persistence, tracking through the yolk sac, brain, and oocytes of the third- (F3) and fourth-generation (F4) descendants derived from the oocyte of AMA progenitors. The transcriptomic data have been deposited in the NCBI Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO) under accession number GSE349634. Processed transcriptomic, lipidomic, and proteomic datasets, together with the shared transcript-protein analysis, have been deposited in RODBUK under DOI https://doi.org/10.57903/UJ/LVQ7FU. All datasets are publicly available. This study was conducted exclusively in a mouse model. Given species-specific variations in baseline oocyte lipid content and developmental kinetics, these findings require cautious interpretation before extrapolation to human clinical contexts. Additionally, the exact molecular and epigenetic mechanisms underlying the intergenerational persistence of these lipid signatures warrant further characterization. These findings demonstrate an association between early-life oocyte lipid changes and downstream pathway-level molecular signatures of neurodevelopmental alterations. By establishing an intergenerational pathway that persists independently of the maternal uterine environment, this work introduces a novel framework linking metabolic programming at conception to neurodevelopmental outcomes, offering new directions for reproductive medicine and translational neuroscience. This research was funded by National Science Centre of Poland Grants 2021/41/B/NZ3/03507 and 2019/35/B/NZ4/03547 (to G.E.P.), 2022/44/C/NZ4/00076 (to M.F.H.), and 2019/35/N/NZ3/03213 (to Ł.G.), and the program 'Excellence initiative-research university' for the AGH University of Krakow (A.B.-K.). Proteomics was supported by the subsidy no 16.16.160.557 of the Polish Ministry of Science and Higher Education (to P.S.). Raman analysis at the National Synchrotron Radiation Centre SOLARIS was supported by the Ministry of Science and Higher Education, Poland, under contract no. 1/SOL/2021/2. The authors declare no competing interests.

title: Astrocytic ADCY8-VEGFA signaling is required for dendritic morphogenesis, neuronal activity and contextual fear memory.
abstract: Contextual fear memory is a hippocampus-dependent and precisely regulated process. Its dysregulation is associated with numerous neuropsychiatric disorders, including post-traumatic stress disorder. However, the mechanisms underlying the expression of this memory remain incompletely elucidated. Here, we provide evidence that astrocytic, rather than neuronal, adenylate cyclase 8 (ADCY8) regulates contextual fear memory. Single-nucleus RNA sequencing analysis suggests that Adcy8-positive astrocytes are more likely to respond to fear conditioning and to modulate synaptic functions. Conditional knockout (CKO) of Adcy8 in astrocytes impairs dendritic morphogenesis, suppresses ventral CA1 (vCA1) neuron activation, and disrupts contextual fear memory retrieval. Further studies identify vascular endothelial growth factor A (VEGFA) as a key downstream effector of ADCY8 in astrocytes, and its expression is substantially decreased in the ventral hippocampus of astrocytic Adcy8 CKO mice by inhibiting the mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK) signaling. Knockdown of Vegfa in vCA1 astrocytes recapitulates the phenotypes observed in astrocytic Adcy8 CKO mice. In contrast, overexpression of Vegfa in vCA1 astrocytes not only rescues contextual fear memory deficits but also reverses the neuronal abnormalities in astrocytic Adcy8 CKO mice. Together, these results reveal a novel role of the astrocytic ADCY8-MAPK-VEGFA axis in governing astrocyte-neuron crosstalk, which is required for dendritic morphogenesis, neuronal activity, and contextual fear memory retrieval.

title: The RNA and protein landscapes of mouse brain organoids.
abstract: Organoids are powerful models of brain development and function. Mouse brain organoids reproduce the main steps of neurodevelopment in vivo and differentiate more rapidly than human organoids, making them scalable for screening applications. However, mouse brain organoids remain poorly defined. Here, we showed that the transcriptome and proteome of mouse brain organoids developed for three weeks are close to those of a neonatal mouse brain. Strikingly, organoids recapitulated the majority of alternative splicing and polyadenylation-site events that define neural identity in vivo. Proteomics revealed that most changes in mRNA expression were translated into proteins. Mouse brain organoids differentiated for only three weeks already harbored a complex network of synaptic proteins, including the ionotropic and metabotropic receptors for the neurotransmitters glutamate and GABA. To conclude, our study provides evidence that mouse brain organoids are a rapidly maturing and relevant model of mammalian brain development and function in a neonatal-like environment.

title: The CsCOP1-CsHY5-CsGGT2 cascade regulates theanine accumulation and functional validation of natural CsGGT2 variants in tea plant.
abstract: Theanine, a signature specialized metabolite unique to tea plants, exerts a decisive influence on tea flavor quality and provides multiple physiological benefits to humans. However, the molecular regulatory mechanisms underlying theanine metabolism, especially the post-translational modification cascades, are still poorly characterized. This work aims to dissect the function of CsCOP1 in modulating theanine metabolism in tea plant, and uncover the post-translational regulatory mechanisms underlying the CsCOP1-CsHY5-CsGGT2 module, along with natural variations in CsGGT2 governing theanine hydrolysis. These findings will provide theoretical underpinnings for breeding high-theanine tea cultivars. The CsCOP1 gene was identified from an albino tea genetic population via quantitative trait locus mapping and weighted gene co-expression network analysis. Transient silencing, transient endogenous overexpression, and heterologous overexpression assays were performed to characterize the biological function of CsCOP1. Protein-protein interaction assays, ubiquitination analyses, and dual-luciferase reporter assays were conducted to verify the physical interaction between CsCOP1 and CsHY5, map the ubiquitination sites of CsHY5, and explore their regulatory effects on CsGGT2 transcription. UPLC and quantitative real-time PCR were adopted to measure theanine content and transcript levels of target genes. Non-synonymous mutations were screened from RNA-sequencing data, and their biological functions were verified using natural tea populations combined with in vitro enzyme activity assays. Silencing CsCOP1 significantly reduced theanine accumulation, whereas overexpression of CsCOP1 markedly elevated theanine content. Mechanistically, CsCOP1 mediated the ubiquitination of CsHY5 at Lys-428. This post-translational modification reduced CsHY5 protein abundance, repressed CsGGT2 transcription, and ultimately attenuated theanine catabolism in tea leaves. Moreover, a non-synonymous mutation in CsGGT2 altered theanine-hydrolyzing activity, and this functional change was validated using natural tea populations. This study established a CsCOP1-centered regulatory network governing theanine metabolism and identified a non-synonymous mutation associated with theanine hydrolysis, laying a theoretical foundation and offering functional molecular markers for breeding high-theanine tea cultivars.

title: Integrative genomic analyses and Fine-Mapping of the 5q31.1 Cytokine Locus Links Food Allergy Risk to Asthma and Atopic Dermatitis Through Shared Causal Variants.
abstract: Food allergy (FA) is a common immune-mediated disorder, yet its genetic architecture and underlying mechanisms remain incompletely understood. We aimed to characterize the genetic architecture of FA, refine association signals through multi-ancestry fine-mapping, and investigate shared genetic and regulatory mechanisms linking FA with asthma and atopic dermatitis (AD). We performed a multi-ancestry GWAS meta-analysis of FA including more than 16,000 cases and over 1 million controls of European, African, and East Asian ancestry. We used sequential conditional analysis and Bayesian fine-mapping to identify independent association signals and prioritize candidate causal variants. We further evaluated shared genetic architecture with asthma and AD through conditional colocalization analysis and integrated FA-associated variants with cis-eQTL and single-nucleus ATAC/RNA-seq data from blood and skin to nominate candidate target genes and disease-relevant cell types. This trans-ancestry design enabled fine-mapping of the 5q31.1 locus (IL4, IL5, and IL13), revealing multiple independent disease-associated signals, including a secondary genome-wide significant variant (rs6873732; p ≤ 5 × 10-8) and a tertiary signal surpassing Bonferroni significance (rs4608913; p = 9.1 × 10-6). Bayesian fine-mapping identified credible causal variants that also associate with asthma and atopic dermatitis (AD). Genetic colocalization demonstrated that the primary FA signal at 5q31.1 aligns with a secondary AD signal (rs11242122), while the secondary and tertiary FA signals at 5q31.1 colocalize with two independent asthma signals (rs12652920 and rs77450473). Outside 5q31.1, we confirmed a genome-wide significant association at 1q21.3 and identified candidate loci at 11q13.5 and 18q21.33-q22.1, each showing strong evidence of shared causal variants (PP > 0.8) with asthma and AD. To connect genetic risk to cellular mechanisms, we integrated single-nucleus ATAC/RNA-seq from blood and skin. At 5q31.1, three variants within the primary credible set overlapped accessible chromatin in basophils and T cells, while seven tertiary-signal variants overlapped open chromatin in basophils, monocytes, keratinocytes, and CD8+ T cells. Integration with cis-eQTL data demonstrated that primary and tertiary FA signals were associated with increased SLC22A5/IL13 expression and upregulation of IRF1, respectively. Together, these findings refine the genetic architecture of FA, reveal shared and disease-specific mechanisms with related allergic diseases, highlight the value of integrating ancestry-diverse GWAS with multi-omics data to prioritize regulatory mechanisms in complex immune-mediated conditions.

title: Identification of circadian rhythm-related diagnostic biomarkers and immune subtypes in allergic rhinitis based on WGCNA and machine learning approaches.
abstract: Allergic rhinitis (AR) is a common chronic inflammatory disease characterized by dysregulated immune responses and pronounced circadian rhythm disturbances. However, the molecular mechanisms linking circadian rhythm-related genes (CRRGs) to AR pathogenesis and immune heterogeneity remain insufficiently understood. Public microarray datasets (GSE75011 and GSE43523) were retrieved from the Gene Expression Omnibus database. Differentially expressed genes (DEGs) between AR patients and healthy controls were identified using the limma package. Circadian rhythm-related DEGs (DECRRGs) were obtained by intersecting DEGs with curated CRRGs. Weighted gene co-expression network analysis (WGCNA) was applied to identify AR-related gene modules. Machine learning algorithms, including support vector machine-recursive feature elimination and Boruta, were used to screen diagnostic biomarkers. Immune infiltration was assessed using CIBERSORT and single-sample Gene Set Enrichment Analysis. Single-gene gene set enrichment analysis, non-negative matrix factorization-based molecular subtyping, and competing endogenous RNA (ceRNA) network construction were subsequently performed. A total of 36 DECRRGs were identified and significantly enriched in immune- and inflammation-related pathways. WGCNA revealed a turquoise module that was strongly correlated with AR. Machine learning analysis identified two key diagnostic biomarkers, BTG1 and IDI1, which demonstrated robust diagnostic performance in both the training set (AUC = 0.781 and 0.755) and the validation set (AUC = 0.986 and 0.857). Immune infiltration analysis revealed significant alterations in immune cell composition between AR and control samples. Non-negative matrix factorization clustering classified AR patients into two distinct molecular subtypes with markedly different immune landscapes. Finally, a ceRNA regulatory network was constructed to elucidate the post-transcriptional regulatory mechanisms of the diagnostic genes. This study systematically identified circadian rhythm-related diagnostic biomarkers for AR and revealed immune-based molecular subtypes, providing novel insights into the circadian-immune regulatory mechanisms underlying AR pathogenesis.

title: Recurrent features of stress response in the unicellular zygnematophyte Mesotaenium: intracellular inclusions and vacuoles forming upon UV.
abstract: The Zygnematophyceae, the closest algal relatives of land plants, many of which are unicellular, must manage environmental stress responses largely cell-autonomously, making them powerful models for dissecting the ancestral cellular toolkit underlying plant terrestrialisation. In this brief report, we revisit UV-B time-course experiment data on the unicellular zygnematophyte Mesotaenium endlicherianum, in which UV-B irradiation triggered a significant accumulation of terminal vacuoles. We re-analysed the corresponding RNA-seq data with a new focus on genes associated with vacuolar biology and lipid metabolism. Within 2 h of UV-B onset, homologs of genes linked to vacuolar functions in land plants were differentially expressed: transcripts of putatively lytic enzymes (a papain-like cysteine protease and two GH38 alpha-mannosidases), of a metal tolerance protein and of two AHK1-like histidine kinases increased, whereas those of the tonoplast H⁺-pyrophosphatase AVP1, the Ca²⁺/H⁺ antiporter CAX5 and the phosphatidylinositol 3-phosphate 5-kinase FAB1A decreased. Lipid-related transcripts indicated a shift from membrane lipid biosynthesis towards lipid turnover, including the induction of a SUGAR-DEPENDENT 1-like triacylglycerol lipase. Based on homology, we propose the working hypothesis that UV-B shifts the vacuole from a homeostatic towards a stress-adapted state with altered ion homeostasis and increased lytic capacity. Together with reports of stress-associated vacuoles in other zygnematophytes, our data are consistent with an ancient role of the vacuole in streptophyte stress responses.

title: Mechanistic insights into lncRNA SNHG6 during the progression of osteoarthritis.
abstract: The present study investigated the role and preliminary regulatory mechanism of the long non-coding RNA small nucleolar RNA host gene 6 (SNHG6) in lipopolysaccharide (LPS)-induced chondrocytes. LPS-induced chondrocytes were used to mimic osteoarthritis (OA) in vitro. Gain- and loss-of-function experiments were performed as follows: the Cell Counting Kit-8 assay for cell viability, flow cytometry for cell cycle and apoptosis analysis, the TUNEL assay for further apoptosis detection, western blotting for apoptosis- and cell cycle-related protein levels, and ELISA for inflammatory cytokine levels. Gene expression levels were detected by reverse transcription-quantitative PCR and immunofluorescence. In LPS-induced chondrocytes and in patients with OA, reduced expression of SNHG6 and PGAP1 as well as increase expression of microRNA (miR)-944 were observed. SNHG6 targets miR-944, and PGAP1 is a target of miR-944. Overexpression of SNHG6 or PGAP1, as well as downregulation of miR-944 markedly suppressed chondrocyte apoptosis and inflammation. Furthermore, increased miR-944 expression reversed the regulatory effects of PGAP1 overexpression in LPS-induced chondrocytes. In conclusion, the role and underlying mechanism of SNHG6 in the progression of OA in vitro were preliminarily identified, and it was found that its overexpression remarkably inhibits chondrocyte apoptosis and inflammation. This regulatory effect may be mediated by regulating the miR-944/PGAP1 axis.

title: Predictors of Long COVID in Adults With Untreated Mild-to-Moderate Coronavirus Disease 2019.
abstract: We evaluated risk factors for long COVID (LC) in the ACTIV-2/A5401 trial, with a focus on understanding the impact of sex. Findings were analyzed in nonhospitalized adults with coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) receiving placebo within 10 days of symptoms. LC was defined as self-reporting COVID-19-related symptoms at study week 24 in a diary. Demographics and clinical variables, nasal viral RNA (vRNA), and inflammatory/coagulation markers were evaluated as predictors of LC, using modified Poisson regression models. Among 545 participants enrolled in January-August 2021 with a week 24 diary, the median age at entry was 44 years, 53% were female, 13% Black, 53% Hispanic/Latino, 83% US enrolled, 15% vaccinated, and 52% severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2) seropositive. Seventy-four (14%) had LC (19% of female and 7% of male participants). Female sex was strongly associated with LC (adjusted risk ratio, 2.64 [95% confidence interval, 1.58-4.42]). Other predictors included US enrollment, higher total symptom score at entry, presence of symptoms at the end of the acute period (days 22-28), 28-day area under the curve of vRNA levels, and higher day 28 C-reactive protein and fibrinogen. The effect of sex persisted with adjustment for the other variables, and associations with symptoms and fibrinogen level varied by sex. In untreated adults with COVID-19, female sex, US enrollment, symptom and vRNA burden, and inflammatory/coagulation measures were associated with increased LC risk, with some associations varying by sex. The association with female sex was not significantly attenuated by adjustment for the assessed biomarkers. These data support sex-stratified investigations of LC, as well as a potential role of thromboinflammation. ClinicalTrials.gov NCT04518410.

title: FABP3 AU modulates bovine intramuscular adipogenesis and is associated with lipid-related metabolic changes.
abstract: Intramuscular fat (IMF) deposition and fatty acid composition are important for beef quality, but the role of antisense long noncoding RNA (lncRNA) in bovine adipogenesis remains unclear. To investigate this, we performed tissue expression analyses, gain- and loss-of-function experiments, multi-omics profiling, and molecular interaction assays to characterize the role of the antisense lncRNA FABP3 AU in bovine adipocyte development. FABP3 AU expression was dynamically regulated during adipocyte differentiation, differed between predefined marbling groups, and showed different relationships with IMF content and fatty acid profiles across age groups. Functional assays supported a role for FABP3 AU in promoting preadipocyte proliferation while suppressing adipocyte differentiation. Integrated transcriptomic and metabolomic analyses suggested that FABP3 AU knockdown was associated with alterations in purine metabolism and protein digestion and absorption pathways. At the mechanistic level, our findings support a model in which FABP3 AU depletion was associated with reduced PABPC1 ubiquitination, increased PABPC1 protein stability, and slower FABP3 mRNA decay. These results suggest that FABP3 AU is an important regulator of bovine intramuscular adipogenesis, providing a basis for future studies into the molecular regulation of intramuscular fat deposition.

title: FOXP3-positive neoplastic TFH cells in nodal TFH lymphoma.
abstract: Nodal T follicular helper (nTFH) lymphomas, including angioimmunoblastic T-cell lymphoma (AITL), are mature T-cell neoplasms characterized by TFH immunophenotypic and transcriptional programs. Here, we report a case of AITL in which the neoplastic TFH population exhibited an unexpected regulatory T-cell phenotype. Through single-cell RNA sequencing we identified a neoplastic T-cell population enriched for TFH gene signatures and co-expressing FOXP3 and other regulatory transcripts. Sequential multiplex immunofluorescence corroborated these findings at the protein level, demonstrating FOXP3, BLIMP1, and CTLA4 expression in cytologically atypical TFH cells. HTLV-1/2 molecular and serologic studies were negative, providing no support for an HTLV-associated process. To our knowledge, this is the first reported case of nTFH lymphoma with a FOXP3-positive neoplastic TFH population exhibiting T follicular regulatory (TFR)-like features, broadening the recognized immunophenotypic spectrum of these lymphomas.

title: Epithelial CD74 regulates intestinal barrier homeostasis.
abstract: CD74, originally identified as the invariant chain of MHC class II, also functions as a receptor for macrophage migration inhibitory factor (MIF). Although CD74 is expressed in various non-lymphoid cells, including epithelial cells across multiple organs, the regulation and functional significance of its expression in these tissues remain poorly understood. Here, we show that CD74 is constitutively expressed in small intestinal epithelial cells, particularly within stem and transit-amplifying compartments, and that its expression is influenced by microbiota and IFN-γ signaling. Conditional deletion of CD74 in IECs (CD74ΔIEC mice) resulted in increased intestinal permeability under steady-state conditions, which was consistent with reduced expression of the tight junction protein ZO-1. While the numbers of intestinal stem cells and Paneth cells remained unchanged, CD74-deficient mice also exhibited elongation of the small intestine and enhanced crypt cell proliferation. Single-cell RNA sequencing revealed enrichment of mitochondrial pathways in CD74-deficient IECs. Consistent with these findings, CD74-deficient IECs exhibited increased mitochondrial content and altered mitochondrial membrane potential. Organoid cultures further showed accelerated growth and increased proliferation in the absence of CD74. Together, these findings suggest that CD74 contributes to intestinal epithelial homeostasis by limiting epithelial proliferation and supporting tight junction integrity, thereby helping to maintain barrier function under steady-state conditions.

title: The p.Ser143Pro lamin A/C mutation leads to dilated cardiomyopathy and activates the unfolded protein response pathway in a knock-in mouse model.
abstract: Dilated cardiomyopathy (DCM) is characterized by progressive ventricular dilation, systolic dysfunction, and an increased risk of arrythmias and sudden cardiac arrest. Variants in the LMNA gene, which encodes the nuclear lamins A and C, have been linked to the familial form of the disease and the founder variant p.Ser143Pro is particularly common among Finnish patients with DCM. To elucidate the complex and poorly understood pathogenic mechanisms behind LMNA-related DCM, we generated a mouse model carrying the p.Ser143Pro mutation in the Lmna gene. All genetically modified mice appeared normal at birth. However, based on echocardiography, necropsy, natriuretic peptide B (Nppb) expression levels, and histopathological data, homozygous males developed progressive left ventricular dilatation, myocardial fibrosis, and cardiac failure after 6 months of age, with all succumbing before 10 months. A reduced disease penetrance was observed in heterozygous male and homozygous female mice, with one-year survival rates of 40% and 60%, respectively. No signs of skeletal myopathy were observed in mice carrying the mutation. Whole-transcriptome RNA sequencing analysis of left ventricular cardiac tissue from asymptomatic two-month-old homozygous male mice revealed an upregulation of classical heart failure markers, such as natriuretic peptide A (Nppa) and myosin heavy chain 7 (Myh7), and an elevated unfolded protein response signaling, as shown by elevated DNA damage inducible transcript 3 (Ddit3), BAG cochaperone 3 (Bag3) and CCAAT enhancer binding protein beta (Cebpb) levels. In conclusion, p.Ser143Pro-Lmna mice closely mimic the clinical phenotype observed in patients with the p.Ser143Pro LMNA variant and offer a valuable in vivo model for investigating the underlying pathogenic mechanisms of LMNA-related DCM. © 2026 The Author(s). The Journal of Pathology published by John Wiley & Sons Ltd on behalf of The Pathological Society of Great Britain and Ireland.

title: Decoding the implicit paradigm of exosome targeting blood brain barrier in neurodegenerative diseases: Molecular insight and therapeutic perspective.
abstract: Exosome physiology in the progression of neurodegenerative diseases is intricately tangled with various protein aggregations, including tau protein, α-synuclein, and amyloid-β protein. Exosomes facilitate therapeutic and prognostic avenues through cell-to-cell crosstalk mechanisms, drug delivery, and biomarker isolation strategies in neurodegenerative disease management. The significant implications of molecular insights into neurofibrillary tangles and synaptic dysfunction have been extensively explored through microRNA (miRNA) regulation. The therapeutic potential of exosomes as nano-cargo systems is significant in nervous tissue regeneration and the treatment of neuronal lesions. Advancements in exosome engineering, including genetic modifications, have expanded their capacity to transport RNA molecules, proteins, and novel gene-editing tools such as CRISPR/Cas9, thereby enabling neuroprotective treatment protocols. Integration with immunotherapeutic approaches further highlights exosomes as promising components of combined strategies with important clinical outcomes.

title: Identification of Key Fatty acid Metabolism-Related Genes in Vascular Dementia.
abstract: Vascular dementia (VaD) is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder characterized by chronic cerebral hypoperfusion and cognitive decline, yet the role of fatty acid metabolism in its pathogenesis remains incompletely understood. Integrated transcriptomic profiling was combined with network-based analysis, weighted gene co-expression network analysis (WGCNA) and machine learning to uncover key fatty acid metabolism-associated molecular features associated with VaD. Single-cell RNA sequencing, intercellular communication inference, and in silico perturbation analyses were applied to define immune-stromal interactions. Potential therapeutic compounds were evaluated using molecular docking and dynamics simulations. We identified three VaD-related fatty acid metabolism genes (VaD-FAMRGs), namely PNPLA3, HSP90AA1, and ALB, which showed consistent diagnostic performance across multiple computational approaches and were associated with lipid metabolism, inflammatory processes, and neurovascular unit dysfunction. Functional enrichment, single-cell RNA sequencing, and in silico gene perturbation analyses provided exploratory insights into the potential associations of these candidate genes with lipid transport, metabolic regulation, synaptic maintenance, and immune-inflammatory processes. Cell-cell communication analysis further revealed activation of the ANGPTL signaling axis, suggesting impaired endothelial-glial interactions driven by lipid metabolic dysregulation. Regulatory network analysis identified key transcriptional and post-transcriptional regulators, including REST, miR-155-5p, and miR-21-5p, which may coordinately modulate VaD-FAMRG expression. Drug repurposing analysis highlighted quercetin as a candidate compound with predicted interactions with all three hub proteins, supported by molecular docking and molecular dynamics simulations. These findings suggest that dysregulated fatty acid metabolism may be associated with the development and progression of VaD through coordinated metabolic, inflammatory, and neurovascular mechanisms. This study provides a systems-level framework for understanding the underlying pathological processes and establishes a theoretical basis for future mechanistic and experimental validation.

title: Low-intensity pulsed ultrasound promotes Rtn3L-associated axonal remodeling and functional recovery after spinal cord injury.
abstract: Spinal cord injury produces persistent neurological dysfunction because injured central axons have limited capacity for structural repair and because secondary tissue changes constrain neural plasticity. Low-intensity pulsed ultrasound is a noninvasive physical stimulation strategy with emerging neuroregenerative potential, but the molecular components associated with its effects after spinal cord injury remain incompletely defined. In a mouse unilateral T9-T10 spinal cord hemisection model, we first compared 30, 45, and 60 mW/cm2 low-intensity pulsed ultrasound and selected 45 mW/cm2 as the working regimen for subsequent experiments. Low-intensity pulsed ultrasound improved locomotor and sensory performance, motor-evoked potential conduction, tractography-based structural features, neurofilament-200-positive axonal organization, and axon-myelin ultrastructure. Labelfree proteomic profiling of lesion-containing spinal cord tissue identified coordinated changes in neural and axon-associated programs and prioritized Rtn3 as a low-intensity pulsed ultrasound-responsive candidate; peptide-level evidence supported the direction of the protein-level change. Exploratory reanalysis of public single-cell RNA-sequencing datasets was used only to provide cell-type context at the Rtn3 transcript level. Subsequent isoform-focused experiments showed that the long Rtn3 isoform, Rtn3L, decreased after injury and was partially restored by low-intensity pulsed ultrasound in vivo and in nerve growth factor-differentiated PC12 cells. Adeno-associated virus-mediated Rtn3L overexpression reproduced several low-intensity pulsed ultrasound-associated behavioral, electrophysiological, imaging, and axon-myelin structural features, whereas Rtn3L knockdown attenuated multiple responses to low-intensity pulsed ultrasound. Parallel gain- and loss-of-function experiments in PC12 cells showed corresponding changes in neurite outgrowth. These findings identify Rtn3L as a functionally relevant contributor to low-intensity pulsed ultrasound-associated axonal remodeling after spinal cord injury.

title: Advanced drug delivery strategies for overcoming tumor-mediated molecular hijacking: Emerging nanotherapeutics, advanced biotherapeutics, and artificial intelligence.
abstract: Recent advances in precision oncology fueled the development of nanotherapeutics,​ molecularly targeted drugs, engineered immunotherapies, RNA therapeutics, and smart biomaterials for more selective cancer treatment. However, long-term therapeutic responses remain restricted by interconnected adaptive mechanisms, including ABC transporter-mediated drug efflux, dysregulated signaling pathways, apoptosis evasion, immune escape, epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition, and tumor microenvironment​ remodeling. In this review article, these processes are collectively framed as tumor-mediated molecular hijacking, describing malignant cell exploitation and microenvironmental pathways that promote multidrug resistance and therapeutic failure. The review critically examines nanotherapeutic and advanced biotherapeutic strategies to counteract these mechanisms, including functionalized nanocarriers, antibody-drug conjugates, CAR-T cells, tumor-infiltrating lymphocyte therapy, immune checkpoint blockade, mesenchymal stem-cell (MSC)-based therapeutics, CRISPR-mediated genome editing, bispecific T-cell engagers, and RNA-based approaches. Particular focus includes drug-delivery elements such as tumour penetration, intracellular trafficking, controlled release, pharmacokinetics, biodistribution, and critical formulation attributes, as well as translational challenges such as manufacturability, scalability, reproducibility, stability, safety, and regulatory feasibility. Emerging biofabrication approaches enable the fabrication of adaptive and personalized delivery systems, while artificial intelligence and machine learning are utilized as tools for structure-guided design, nanocarrier optimization, treatment-response prediction, and patient-specific digital-twin modelling. This paper combines tumor-mediated molecular hijacking with drug delivery technology at the forefront and translational aspects to create a comprehensive platform for clinically relevant precision cancer therapeutics.Clinical trial number: Not applicable.

title: Microplastics (MPs)-associated chemical components are associated with hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) progression via genomic instability and spatial microenvironment remodeling: A study based on integrated multi-omics analysis.
abstract: Microplastics (MPs) and their toxic components (BPA, DBP, DEHP) pose global health threats, with the liver as primary target. The mechanisms by which MPs may contribute to hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) progression and spatial microenvironment remodeling remain poorly understood. We employed an integrated multi-omics workflow combining bulk transcriptomics, WGCNA, ten machine learning algorithms combined into 101 candidate model combinations, single-cell RNA-seq, spatial transcriptomics (ST), inferCNV, CytoTRACE, and molecular docking with 100 ns molecular dynamics (MD) simulations. We identified 22 hub genes at the putative intersection of HCC dysregulation and documented toxicological targets of MP-associated chemicals (BPA, DBP, and DEHP), enriched in cell cycle and senescence. A 6-gene (AKR1C3, AURKA, CCNB1, EZH2, FABP5, ESR1) risk model (glmBoost + SVM) achieved high diagnostic accuracy (mean external AUC = 0.965; internal bootstrap validation of the six-gene logistic model: bias-corrected AUC = 0.987 (optimism = 0.005). Single-cell analysis revealed risk genes localized in HCC parenchymal and myeloid cells, putatively positively correlating with CNV burden and stemness, while ESR1 showed inverse correlation. ST suggested spatial expression gradients of AKR1C3 and FABP5 with increasing malignancy. Molecular docking of all six hub targets against BPA, DBP, and DEHP, followed by 100 ns MD simulations of the AKR1C3-ligand complexes-the biologically most relevant sub-network-suggested structurally stable binding, with RMSD fluctuations (0.13-0.5 nm), maintained hydrogen bonds, stable Rg and SASA, low RMSF, and favorable free energy landscapes, supporting the structural plausibility of protein-ligand interactions. This study provides a multidimensional, hypothesis-generating landscape of HCC progression associated with MP-associated chemical exposure at single-cell and spatial resolutions, with dynamic and energetic evidence supporting the structural plausibility of stable plasticizer-target binding, offering novel toxicological targets and mechanistic insights for environmental and clinical intervention.

title: Beyond monoamines: a multi-systems molecular framework for major depressive disorder.
abstract: For over five decades, the monoamine hypothesis has anchored the conceptual and pharmacological approach to major depressive disorder (MDD), yet nearly one-third of patients fail to achieve remission with standard antidepressants, and therapeutic response is delayed by weeks. This narrative review offers a critical synthesis of recent high-impact literature drawn on evidence from genomic, molecular, and translational studies across six domains: genomic architecture, epigenetic dysregulation, neuroinflammation, neurotrophic signalling, gut-brain axis, and rapid-acting antidepressant mechanisms, to construct a multi-systems framework of MDD pathophysiology and, as a secondary and explicitly scoped aim, to identify translational priorities for South Asian, particularly Indian, populations; the evidence reviewed is global in scope. A 2025 genome-wide association study (GWAS) of 688,808 cases identified 697 independent associations mapping to 635 genomic risk loci implicating glutamatergic, GABAergic, and neuropeptidergic systems. Environmental stressors converge on this genetic susceptibility through DNA methylation, histone modification, and non-coding RNA-mediated epigenetic reprogramming. An inflammatory MDD subgroup, characterised by kynurenine pathway disruption and microglial dysregulation, is of interest for patient stratification. Rapid-acting antidepressants proposed to act through TrkB-BDNF-dependent synaptic plasticity offer a mechanistic account of their fast onset, although the direct-binding theory awaits independent replication. Gut microbiome dysbiosis, particularly among neurotransmitter-producing taxa, further extends the pathophysiological map beyond the brain itself. Together, these findings support a shift from a unidimensional monoaminergic model to an integrated, multi-systems molecular framework of MDD. Realising the clinical potential of this framework will require validated precision biomarker panels, dedicated South Asian GWAS cohorts, and longitudinal multi-omics studies.

title: CDKN3 in cancer: context-dependent cell-cycle control and implications for genome stability and therapy.
abstract: Cyclin-dependent kinase inhibitor 3 (CDKN3), also known as kinase-associated phosphatase (KAP), dephosphorylates activating cyclin-dependent kinase 2 (CDK2) Thr160, yet high expression is associated with aggressive features in some cancers. This review distinguishes messenger RNA (mRNA) expression, protein abundance, phosphatase activity, functional dependency, prognostic association, and treatment-response prediction. Renal studies include selected perturbation evidence, whereas lung studies cited here primarily report prognostic or computational associations. Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) findings remain directionally discordant across analytes, etiologies, models, and endpoints. Recent triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC) studies include transcriptomic and cell-perturbation evidence, as well as a separate cell and murine mammary fat-pad graft study, while an ultraviolet (UV)-induced skin-cancer study identifies a sex- and context-specific protective axis. These results do not support a universal CDKN3 role. A CDKN3-specific connection to chromosomal instability (CIN) and cyclic GMP-AMP synthase (cGAS)-stimulator of interferon genes (STING) signaling remains unvalidated. Micronuclei and CIN do not invariably activate cGAS-STING. Bulk immune signatures and survival associations alone cannot establish direct immune regulation, functional dependency, or treatment sensitivity. This focused narrative review compares molecular measurements, genetic perturbations, clinical associations, and selected computational studies. We outline matched assays, genetic rescue, longitudinal CIN measurements, and pathway-specific tests needed to determine whether CDKN3 is a context-specific dependency, a biomarker, or a therapeutic target.

title: Dibutyl phthalate at environmentally relevant concentrations promotes hepatocellular carcinoma progression via stabilization of hepatocyte-derived lipocalin-2.
abstract: Dibutyl phthalate (DBP) is a ubiquitous environmental contaminant whose exposure is positively associated with the progression of metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD). However, the underlying mechanisms by which DBP promotes MASLD progression remain unclear. In this study, high-throughput RNA sequencing revealed that the DBP-orchestrated liver transcriptome is enriched in target clusters associated with hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC), an advanced complication of MASLD. DBP promotes HCC progression in murine models but does not directly affect HCC cell proliferation, indicating that hepatocytes may be the primary target cells for DBP signaling. To identify a molecular target in hepatocytes that transduces DBP signals to HCC cells, we performed label-free proteomic analyses, molecular docking, and the Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA) database analyses, which identified hepatocyte-derived lipocalin-2 (LCN2) as a candidate target of DBP. Elevated LCN2 expression is negatively associated with overall survival in HCC patients. Inhibition of LCN2 partially attenuates the tumor-promoting effect of DBP-treated hepatocytes on HCC cells. Mechanistically, molecular docking and molecular dynamics simulations demonstrate that DBP directly binds to LCN2 to form a stable complex, which disrupts ubiquitin-proteasome-mediated degradation of LCN2 and thereby enhances its protein stability. Functionally, hepatocyte-derived LCN2 promotes HCC cell proliferation through activation of the 24p3R-matrix metalloproteinase-9 (MMP-9) signaling axis. Our findings demonstrate that DBP acts as a progression promoter in pre-existing HCC via hepatocyte LCN2 stabilization, rather than an initiator of hepatocarcinogenesis. This mechanistic insight addresses a critical gap in understanding how environmental toxicants modulate established HCC progression, complementing epidemiological associations between phthalates and liver disease.

title: Nanopore direct RNA sequencing reveals the 2'-O-methylation landscape and SNORD88B-guided FN1 modification in hepatocellular carcinoma.
abstract: To systematically map the internal 2'-O-methylation (Nm) landscape on messenger RNA (mRNA) in hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC), characterize its distribution features and biological functions, and identify key C/D box small nucleolar RNAs (snoRNAs) that regulate Nm modification along with their target genes, thereby providing a molecular basis for elucidating post-transcriptional regulatory mechanisms in HCC. Based on Nanopore direct RNA sequencing data from the HepG2 cell line, we employed the NanoNm machine learning algorithm to systematically identify internal Nm modification sites on mRNA and analyzed their sequence preferences, genomic distribution, and methylation ratio characteristics. Gene Ontology (GO) and Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG) enrichment analyses were then performed to explore the biological functions of the modified genes. Using snoRNA expression profiles from the GSE233521 dataset derived from liver cancer stem cells, we conducted differential expression analysis to screen for significantly differentially expressed C/D box snoRNAs. Based on the principle of sequence complementarity, we predicted their guided Nm-modified target genes. Subsequently, hepatocellular carcinoma single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) data were used to characterize the cell-type-specific expression of the target genes. A total of 10,450 high-confidence consensus Nm modification sites were identified, spanning 1515 genes. These modification sites exhibited a significant sequence preference for AGmA and UCmU trinucleotide motifs (where "m" denotes 2'-O-methylation). Genes bearing Nm modifications were significantly enriched in pathways associated with energy metabolism and protein synthesis, including oxidative phosphorylation, ribosome assembly, and cytoplasmic translation. SNORD88B was significantly upregulated in liver cancer stem cells, its guide sequence displayed perfect base-pairing complementarity with the Nm-modified region of fibronectin 1 (FN1) mRNA. Furthermore, single-cell RNA sequencing analysis revealed that FN1 was specifically expressed in hepatocellular carcinoma tumor cell clusters. This study systematically mapped the global landscape of internal Nm modifications on HCC mRNA at single-base resolution. Nm modification may participate in the development and progression of HCC by modulating the expression and function of target genes. The high expression of SNORD88B in liver cancer stem cells may promote the malignant progression of HCC by guiding Nm modification on FN1 mRNA, thereby providing new research directions for an in-depth understanding of the regulatory mechanisms of snoRNA-mediated Nm modification in HCC.

title: Multilayer Transcriptomic Analysis Prioritizes RAE1 and SLC25A46 as Alzheimer's Disease Candidate Genes Related to Nucleocytoplasmic Transport and Mitochondrial Homeostasis.
abstract: Regional and cellular heterogeneity complicates transcriptomic candidate prioritization in Alzheimer's disease (AD). We integrated donor-adjusted differential expression, exploratory co-expression analysis, donor-grouped nested machine learning, external evaluation, and single-nucleus and spatial localization. Differential screening used false discovery rate < 0.05 and absolute log2 fold change > 0.10. We also examined functional enrichment, immune context, pseudotime, cell communication, virtual knockout, and exploratory compound screening and docking. Among 173 tissue samples from 63 donors, 356 genes met the screening criteria; 44 of 113 algorithm combinations yielded complete evaluations. RAE1 was downregulated across four discovery regions and both external cohorts, with areas under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) of 0.662 (95% confidence interval 0.429-0.894) and 0.863 (0.693-1.000). The frozen Stepglm[forward] model yielded external AUCs of 0.5154 and 0.8875. SLC25A46 showed opposite discovery and external expression directions. Genome-wide enrichment identified 754 Gene Ontology terms and 62 Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes pathways, including negatively enriched mitochondrial energy and RNA-processing programs. Localization across 61,472 nuclei and 25,293 spatial spots, together with virtual perturbation, defined cellular contexts. R-547, JNJ-7,706,621, and roscovitine provided single-engine docking leads. These findings prioritize RAE1 for nucleocytoplasmic RNA-transport research and SLC25A46 as a context-dependent mitochondrial-homeostasis candidate. The compound results provide leads for target-binding and cellular functional studies.

title: Biologic Treatment Outcomes and the Biomarker Potential of Plasma MMP9 in Generalized Pustular Psoriasis: A Real-World Study.
abstract: Generalized pustular psoriasis (GPP) is a severe neutrophilic inflammatory disease. Although biologics targeting IL-17A, IL-12/23, and IL-36R are used in clinical practice, their relative effectiveness in real-world has not been fully characterized, and the potential value of plasma MMP9 as a biomarker of disease activity remains unclear. To compare differences in efficacy and safety among biologics targeting IL-17A, IL-12/23, and IL-36R, and to evaluate changes in treatment-related plasma MMP9 levels and their association with disease activity and routine laboratory markers. Additionally, to characterize the cellular expression patterns of MMP9 in GPP lesions using single-cell transcriptomic analysis. This retrospective study included patients with GPP who received IL-17A, IL-12/23, or IL-36R inhibitors between July 2019 and May 2025. Clinical outcomes were evaluated over 24 weeks. Plasma MMP9 levels were measured longitudinally and correlated with clinical activity and inflammatory markers. Single-cell RNA sequencing of GPP lesions was performed to characterize the cellular expression pattern of MMP9. A total of 72 patients were included in the clinical effectiveness analysis. After 24 weeks, GPP Area and Severity Index (GPPASI), GPP physician global assessment (GPPGA), and Dermatology Life Quality Index (DLQI) improved significantly from baseline, with IL-36R inhibitors showing the most rapid response, followed by IL-17A and IL-12/23 inhibitors. In patients with available plasma samples (n=13), baseline MMP9 showed the strongest observed correlation with GPPASI among the assessed index (Spearman's r = 0.8736, P<0.001), whereas the correlations of GPPASI with C-reactive protein (CRP), white blood cell count (WBC), neutrophil count, and albumin were relatively weak. Single-cell RNA sequencing revealed predominant MMP9 expression in myeloid cells, particularly neutrophils and macrophages. Biologics targeting IL-36R, IL-17A, and IL-12/23 provided sustained disease control in GPP. Circulating MMP9 was strongly associated with GPPASI, decreased following biologic treatment, and exhibited a predominantly myeloid expression pattern in GPP lesions, supporting its further evaluation as a candidate disease-activity biomarker.

title: Targeting AP1S1 modulates the unfolded protein response and cell cycle and sensitizes triple-negative breast cancer to erlotinib.
abstract: Triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC) is an aggressive malignancy lacking actionable therapeutic targets. Intrinsic resistance to tyrosine kinase inhibitor (TKI) therapy remains a major barrier to improving clinical outcomes. Here, we identify adaptor-related protein complex 1 subunit sigma 1 (AP1S1) as an oncogenic regulator and a potential therapeutic vulnerability in TNBC. Through integrated multi-omics profiling and experimental validation, we found that AP1S1 is significantly overexpressed in breast cancer and correlates with advanced clinicopathological features and poor prognosis. Functionally, knockdown of AP1S1 inhibited cell proliferation, induced apoptosis, and triggered cell cycle arrest in vitro and in patient-derived organoids (PDOs). Single-cell RNA sequencing quantitatively confirmed that AP1S1 expression is specifically enriched in malignant cell populations and closely associates with hyperproliferation and stress-response pathways. Molecularly, AP1S1 is involved in a functional network involving both cell cycle progression and the unfolded protein response (UPR), and its high expression correlates with an "immune-desert" microenvironment characterized by depleted effector T cell infiltration. Furthermore, integrating pharmacogenomic analysis with in vitro and PDOs assays, we found that AP1S1 depletion increases the sensitivity of TNBC cells to erlotinib. Collectively, these findings identify AP1S1 as a multifaceted regulator of TNBC aggressiveness and therapy responsiveness, highlighting its potential as a therapeutic target to enhance TKI sensitivity and its association with immune exclusion.

title: Prognostic biomarker SCNM1 is associated with immune infiltration and therapeutic response, and promotes tumor migration in hepatocellular carcinoma.
abstract: Sodium channel modifier 1 (SCNM1) is involved in biological processes including RNA splicing and the regulation of primary cilium length; however, its role in hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) remains largely unclear. The present study aimed to investigate the expression pattern, clinical relevance and functional significance of SCNM1 in HCC. Clinical and transcriptomic data were obtained from The Cancer Genome Atlas, Genotype-Tissue Expression, International Cancer Genome Consortium and Gene Expression Omnibus databases. SCNM1 expression, DNA methylation status and immune infiltration characteristics were systematically analyzed. A SCNM1-related prognostic gene signature was constructed using machine learning approaches. Cell Counting Kit-8, colony formation and Transwell migration assays were performed to evaluate the effects of SCNM1 knockdown on Huh1 cell proliferation, clonogenic capacity and migration, respectively. SCNM1 protein expression was also evaluated by immunohistochemistry in clinical tissue specimens obtained from 10 patients with HCC. SCNM1 was significantly upregulated in HCC tissues and was associated with unfavorable survival outcomes. Immunohistochemical staining further confirmed higher SCNM1 protein expression in HCC tissues than in non-tumor liver tissues. Gene set enrichment analysis indicated that SCNM1 expression was closely associated with metabolic pathways, including oxidative phosphorylation and immune-related processes. Elevated SCNM1 expression was associated with increased estimated infiltration of immune cells, including B cells and macrophages, and positively correlated with the expression of antigen processing and presentation-related genes, including human leukocyte antigen-A, transporter associated with antigen processing (TAP)1 and TAP2. Functional experiments demonstrated that SCNM1 knockdown suppressed HCC cell proliferation, clonogenic capacity and migratory ability. In addition, the SCNM1-based prognostic model effectively stratified patients with distinct survival outcomes. In conclusion, the results indicated that SCNM1 is upregulated in HCC and is associated with poor prognosis and immune-related characteristics. The SCNM1-related prognostic model may provide a useful tool for patient risk stratification and offer insights into the clinical relevance of SCNM1 in HCC.

title: Single-cell multiomics profiling reveals tumour microenvironment landscape and sex-specific immune-suppressive feature in male breast cancer.
abstract: Male breast cancer (MBC) represents a small proportion of all breast cancer (BC) cases, yet it is characterized by a higher rate of lymph node metastasis and poorer prognosis compared to female breast cancer (FBC). However, limited research has been conducted on MBC primarily due to its rarity and the technological constraints. To address this, we performed single-nucleus RNA sequencing (snRNA-seq) on samples from 16 MBC patients (87 518 cells) and imaging mass cytometry (IMC) on samples from 42 patients (265 137 cells), enabling a comprehensive analysis of the MBC microenvironment at both single-cell transcriptome and protein levels. At the autosomal level, the MBC tumor cells and their microenvironment exhibit distinct characteristics. We found that PDZ binding kinase (PBK) expression was elevated in MBC tumor cells and linked to proliferation-related programs, whereas SRY-Box transcription factor 4 (SOX4) expression was increased in endothelial cells and associated with endothelial-mesenchymal transition (EndMT) signatures and metastatic potential. Additionally, IMC analysis revealed notable differences in the spatial features of the tumor microenvironment between MBC and FBC. Regarding sex-chromosomal regulation, the lysine demethylase 5D (KDM5D) gene originating from the Y chromosome was associated with cGAS/STING protein abundance and reduced immune cell infiltration in MBC. In conclusion, both autosomal and sex-chromosomal regulation may collectively contribute to the modulation of microenvironmental differences between MBC and FBC. Whether KDM5D is functionally linked to cGAS/STING signaling requires further validation. Our findings provide insights into the unique microenvironment and clinical manifestations of MBC and generate hypotheses for future functional studies. Multi-omics profiling reveals a distinct, relatively immune-cold microenvironment in male breast cancer. PBK expression is associated with proliferation programs in MBC epithelial cells. SOX4 expression in endothelial cells is linked to an EndMT-like phenotype. KDM5D-low status is associated with reduced cGAS/STING protein levels and immune infiltration.

title: Distinct cellular source and bulk immune correlates of HAVCR2 expression in seminoma.
abstract: HAVCR2 (T-cell immunoglobulin and mucin domain-containing protein 3; TIM-3) expression is associated with favorable prognosis in seminoma, but its underlying immune context remains unclear. We sought to distinguish the cellular source of HAVCR2 from the immune correlates of its interpatient bulk expression using bulk and single-cell transcriptomic datasets. In The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA) seminoma discovery cohort (n = 64), we evaluated associations between HAVCR2 expression and eight predefined immune-compartment signatures, adjusting for overall immune infiltration using PTPRC (CD45) and the ESTIMATE algorithm. After adjustment, associations with T-cell-, cytotoxicity-, and checkpoint-related signatures were attenuated or lost, whereas macrophage-related signatures remained correlated with HAVCR2 expression; on mutual adjustment, the general macrophage rather than the M2-associated signature retained this association. In an independent bulk cohort (GSE3218, n = 13), the M2-associated signature remained associated with HAVCR2 after PTPRC adjustment, whereas the general macrophage association was directionally concordant but attenuated after adjustment. Single-cell RNA sequencing of a four-donor seminoma cohort (GSE228501) showed background-level HAVCR2 expression in tumor cells, while HAVCR2-positive cells were detected in macrophage, exhaustion-like CD8 T-cell, and proliferating T-cell compartments, with donor-level mean expression numerically higher in exhaustion-like CD8 T cells than in macrophages. Although HAVCR2 was expressed across multiple immune compartments at the single-cell level, interpatient bulk HAVCR2 expression was associated with a macrophage-related immune context beyond overall immune infiltration, whereas the specific macrophage phenotype remained unresolved. These findings inform the interpretation of bulk HAVCR2 as a biomarker, including its previously reported prognostic association, without implying a causal role for macrophages in clinical outcome.
